items.title: [FDD Diary #13] Fix One, Break Three
content:
Fixed the double notification.
Then the logs stopped.

Fixed the logs.
Then user settings got reset.

Fixed user settings.
Notifications fire three times.

Worse than before.

Pulled one end of a tangled thread.
The other side tightened.
Three spots tangled at once.
The more you pull, the worse it gets.

How did it get this way?

Built notification code. Needed the user's name. Pulled from user code. Natural.
Built agent code. Agent finishes, sends notification. Pulled from notification. Natural.
Built user settings. Turn off notifications per agent. Pulled from agent code. Natural.

Each step was "natural."
But three steps form a circle.
A -> B -> C -> A.
Circular dependency. No starting point.

I didn't create the bugs.
The structure is the bug.

Each line of code is correct.
Each feature works on its own.
But everything is tangled together.

SDD nailed "what to build."
But "where to put it" was never decided.
Never asked that question.
Never asked, so the code tangled itself.

Structure rots when you don't define it.

items.title: [FDD Diary #14] No Name, No Direction
content:
An apartment with no walls.
Kitchen is the bedroom is the bathroom.

Cook something. Grease splatters on the bed.
Shower. The sofa gets wet.
Do anything anywhere. Something else gets hit.

No walls, so it looks like freedom.
"I can cook anywhere!"
Is that freedom?

No. That's chaos.
Walls seem inconvenient.
But grease doesn't splatter.

`getNotificationConfig`.
Name says notification.
But inside, it's reading the user database directly.
Is this notification or user?

`sendAgentAlert`.
Name says agent alert.
Inside, it reads user settings, writes logs, sends notification.
One function doing three worlds.

"Just" grab it. Those four letters are the problem.
"Just" means no walls.
No walls means anything tangles.

Each world has its own language.

Agent world: "task," "execution," "result."
User world: "account," "permission," "settings."
Notification world: "channel," "message," "dispatch."

Name things precisely.
If the name fits, it's in the right place.
If it doesn't fit, you're sleeping in the kitchen.

They call this DDD. Domain-Driven Design.
SDD nailed "what to build."
DDD nails "where to put it."

items.title: [FDD Diary #15] Building Walls
content:
"Split this code by domain."
Agent world. User world. Notification world.

First file moved. Broke immediately.
Notification code was reading user database directly.
"If I move this, I can't see the user code."

Obviously. You moved to a different world.
When you shared a room, you just reached over.
Put up a wall and your arm doesn't reach.

Every wall I built, hidden wires came out.
The tangled stuff runs silently.
Separate it and it snaps.

So I made interfaces.

"All I need from you is this one thing."

Notification needs the user's name.
Can't read the database directly. Different world.
"Give me the user's name." User world hands it over.
Notification doesn't know how it was fetched.
Not knowing is correct.

That's a contract.
"I need only this. You give only this."

No walls, every change ripples everywhere.
Walls up, changes stop at the wall.

But walls alone weren't enough.
The AI jumped over them.

"I needed this data so I accessed it directly."
"For efficiency."

Efficiency? Reaching over the wall to open someone else's fridge?

That's when Rust saved me.
In Rust, private is private. The compiler blocks you.
AI tries to jump the wall. Doesn't compile.
"This field is private."

Say it in words, it evaporates.
Write it in the environment, it stays.
The compiler is the law.
